To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ACE2/ACE ratio is altered in circulating leukocytes from patients with CKD, and that this imbalance may be involved in the pathogenesis and development of atherosclerotic lesions in these patients.
the ACE/ACE2 ratio in leukocytes is a novel biomarker of cardiovascular disease in chronic kidney disease and can be used as a therapeutic target.
ACE2 is a negative regulator of atherosclerosis, and that ACE2‐overexpression in monocytes leads to a decrease in endothelial adhesion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel mechanism of uremia‐induced atherogenesis, which is mediated by ACE2.
the role of the ACE/ACE2 system and related receptors in atherosclerosis of chronic kidney disease.
the role of ACE/ACE 2 in atherogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ACE2 is an important factor for the development of atherogenesis in CKD.
monocytic ACE2 relates to atherogenesis in patients with CKD.
ACE2 is the most important factor to be targeted in CKD and HD patients to prevent atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
monocytic ACE2 may be a potential therapeutic target to prevent or treat atherosclerosis in chronic kidney disease.
ACE2 is a protective factor in atherogenesis, which may be used for future therapeutic interventions.
ACE‐overexpression in monocytes leads to an increase in AngII and a decrease of ACE2.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ACE2 is a key regulator of monocytic phenotype and behaviour in chronic kidney disease.
the balance of ACE and ACE2 expression on monocytic cells may be an independent risk factor of cardiovascular complications in CKD.
ACE‐mediated downregulation of ACE2 may be a potential therapeutic target in the treatment of atherosclerosis in CKD patients.
